visual.lectureScript:
Hello! This is Unit 11.
In this unit, you ask for things.
You say what you will do.
You say the time.
And you take a train or a taxi.
Listen.
Can I borrow your pen?
Sure. Here you are.
Thanks!
Can I asks: is it OK for me?
Can I sit here? OK.
Can I have a ticket, please? Here you are.
Can you asks a person to do a thing.
Can you help me, please? Sure.
Can you lend me your phone? Sorry, no.
Here you are: say it when you give a thing.
Borrow and lend. Listen.
I borrow your pen. I take it for a short time.
You lend me your pen. You give it for a short time.
Now will.
Say what you will do later.
I will call you. I'll call you.
She will send an email. She'll send an email.
With will, the word does not change.
No s, no e d, no to.
I'll call. She'll call. They'll call.
Am, is and are change to be.
I am late today. Tomorrow I'll be early.
Can you help me? Sure. I'll help you.
Now clock times. Look at a clock.
Six o'clock.
Quarter past six.
Half past six.
Quarter to seven.
A clock time takes at.
The train is at half past six.
I'll call you at eight o'clock.
At is for night, too. I work at night.
And at the weekend.
Now short forms.
We're coming. They're waiting. She's calling a taxi.
Are you coming? Yes, I am.
Are you coming? No, I'm not.
Is he waiting? No, he isn't.
Are they working? No, they aren't.
A yes answer is long. Yes, I am. Not: yes, I'm.
Now listen and do.
Look at a clock, or at your phone.
Say the time.
Now say: I'll call you at, and the time.
Last, two things to say when you stop to find a word.
One moment, please.
Wait a minute, please.
And two things to say when you do not hear.
Sorry? Can you say that again?
Can you speak slowly, please?
Now go to Words. See you soon!

Lena: Hello Ivan! Are you coming to the station?

readings.passageScript:
How to take a train.
1. Look at the time of your train. Go to the station early.
2. Go to the ticket desk. Say: Can I have a ticket to the city, please?
3. Listen to the price. Pay, and say thanks.
4. Look at the station clock and the train times. Is your train late?
5. Wait for your train. Get on, and sit.
Your train leaves at its time. It doesn't wait for you!
No ticket? You can't get on the train.

grammar.title: Can I borrow your pen? Asking and saying OK
grammar.explanation:
Can I…? asks: is it OK for me?
Can you…? asks a person to do a thing.
Say please. It is kind.
Answer: Here you are. OK. Sure. Or: Sorry, no.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Ask for a thing:
Can I have a ticket, please? — Here you are.
Can I borrow your pen? — Sure. Here you are.

Ask to do a thing:
Can I sit here? — OK.
Can I open the window? — Sure.

Ask a person to do a thing:
Can you help me, please? — Sure.
Can you lend me your phone? — Sorry, no.

Offer help:
Can I help you? — Yes, please.

Here you are: you give the thing.
OK, Sure: yes.

Can you swim? asks about you.
Can you help me? asks for help.
grammar.workedExample:
You have got no pen. The person next to you has got a pen.
1. You take it for a short time: borrow.
2. It is for you: Can I …?
3. Can I borrow your pen?
4. Add please: Can I borrow your pen, please?
5. The person gives it: Here you are.
6. You say: Thanks!
grammar.commonMistake:
It is easy to leave out can.
No: I open the window?
Yes: Can I open the window?
No: You help me, please?
Yes: Can you help me, please?
grammar.memoryTip: Can I: for me. Can you: you do it for me.
grammar.practice:
Write Can I or Can you.
1. ___ borrow your pen? — Here you are.
2. ___ help me, please? — Sure.
3. ___ sit next to you? — OK.
4. ___ lend me your phone? — Sorry, no.
5. ___ have a ticket, please? — Here you are.
6. ___ call a taxi for me? — Sure.
7. ___ bring my sister? — OK.
8. ___ send me the email? — Sure.
grammar.answerKey:
1. Can I  2. Can you  3. Can I  4. Can you  5. Can I  6. Can you  7. Can I  8. Can you
Wrong on 4? Lend me: the person gives it to you. So: Can you lend me …?
Borrow is for you: Can I borrow …?

grammar.title: I'll call you: will for later and tomorrow
grammar.explanation:
Say what you will do, later or tomorrow.
Use will, then call, send or bring.
No -s, no -ed, no to.
Say it short: I will is I'll.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
I will call you. — I'll call you.
You will like it. — You'll like it.
She will send an email. — She'll send an email.
He will bring the tickets. — He'll bring the tickets.
We will take a taxi. — We'll take a taxi.
They will come soon. — They'll come soon.

am, is, are: with will, say be.
I'll be late.
The train will be at the station at six.

Offer and promise:
Can you help me? — Sure. I'll help you.
My bag is big. — I'll carry it.
grammar.workedExample:
Your friend asks: Can you send me the photo?
Say what you will do.
1. You will send it later: will.
2. I will send: I'll send.
3. Send: no -s, no -ed, no to.
4. Sure. I'll send it later.
grammar.commonMistake:
It is easy to put to with will.
No: I'll to call you.
Yes: I'll call you.
It is easy to add -s.
No: She'll sends it.
Yes: She'll send it.
grammar.memoryTip: I'll call. She'll call. Not calls, not to call.

grammar.answerKey:
1. will call or 'll call  2. will send or 'll send  3. will be or 'll be  4. will help or 'll help  5. will bring or 'll bring  6. will come  7. will open or 'll open
Wrong on 3? With will, am, is and are change to be: we'll be.
Wrong on 2? No -s with will: she'll send, not she'll sends.

grammar.title: At six o'clock, at night: at for clock times
grammar.explanation:
Say the time of a thing with at.
at six o'clock, at half past six.
At is for night, too: at night.
And for the weekend: at the weekend.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
6:00 — six o'clock
6:15 — quarter past six, or six fifteen
6:30 — half past six, or six thirty
6:45 — quarter to seven, or six forty-five

The train is at six o'clock.
I'll call you at half past seven.
The shop closes at quarter to nine.
I work at night.
We meet at the weekend.

a day: on Monday
morning, afternoon, evening: in the morning
a clock time: at six
On Monday at six o'clock.
grammar.workedExample:
When is the train? The clock says 7:45.
1. 45 minutes is three quarters of an hour.
2. Fifteen minutes to 8:00. Say: quarter to eight.
3. A clock time takes at.
4. The train is at quarter to eight.
grammar.commonMistake:
It is easy to use on or in.
No: The bus is on six o'clock.
Yes: The bus is at six o'clock.
No: I work in night.
Yes: I work at night.
grammar.memoryTip: A clock time: at. At six, at half past six.

grammar.title: We're coming. No, they aren't: short forms with -ing
grammar.explanation:
Say it short: I'm coming. They're waiting.
A no answer can be short: No, I'm not.
A yes answer is long: Yes, I am.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
I am: I'm — I'm coming.
you are: you're — You're late!
he is: he's — He's waiting.
she is: she's — She's calling a taxi.
it is: it's — It's coming now.
we are: we're — We're at the station.
they are: they're — They're working.

is not: isn't — The bus isn't coming.
are not: aren't — They aren't waiting.

Are you coming? Yes, I am. No, I'm not.
Is she working? Yes, she is. No, she isn't.
Are they waiting? Yes, they are. No, they aren't.
grammar.workedExample:
Are Ana and Ben coming?
The answer is no. Use a short form.
1. Ana and Ben: they.
2. They are not: they aren't.
3. No, they aren't.
4. Add a line: They're working.
grammar.commonMistake:
It is easy to make a yes answer short.
No: Are you coming? Yes, I'm.
Yes: Are you coming? Yes, I am.
A no answer can be short: No, I'm not.
grammar.memoryTip: Yes: long. No: short. Yes, I am. No, I'm not.

grammar.answerKey:
1. I am  2. he isn't  3. they aren't  4. it is  5. I'm not  6. she is  7. We're waiting at the clock.  8. She isn't coming today.
Wrong on 1, 4 or 6? A yes answer is long: Yes, I am. Not: Yes, I'm.
Wrong on 3? They are not: they aren't.
